lesson.title: Rebuilding a Broken Union: Competing Reconstruction Plans
lesson.summary: Before Congress took control of Reconstruction, Lincoln and then Andrew Johnson each tried lenient approaches to readmitting the former Confederate states, plans whose failures set the stage for a far more radical policy.
lesson.body:
Even before the Civil War ended, Union leaders faced a question with no clear precedent: how should the Confederate states be brought back into the Union, and on what terms. Abraham Lincoln offered his answer first. In December 1863, he issued the Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction, often called the Ten Percent Plan, which offered pardons to most Confederates who swore an oath of loyalty to the Union and accepted the end of slavery, and allowed a state to form a new government once just ten percent of its 1860 voters had taken that oath. Lincoln's plan grew directly out of the Emancipation Proclamation's logic. He hoped a lenient approach would encourage Southern Unionists and war weary Confederates to abandon the rebellion early, shortening the war, while still requiring acceptance of emancipation as a nonnegotiable condition for any state's return.

Many Republicans in Congress thought this was far too soft. The Radical Republicans believed that a rebellion responsible for four years of war and hundreds of thousands of deaths should not be forgiven so easily, and that a ten percent threshold would let the old planter elite simply reclaim power under a new name. In July 1864, Congress passed the Wade Davis Bill, which required a majority, not just ten percent, of a state's voters to take a stricter ironclad oath swearing they had never voluntarily supported the Confederacy, a bar many former Confederates could not honestly meet. Lincoln refused to sign it before Congress adjourned, killing it with a pocket veto, and the dispute between the president and Congress over how strict Reconstruction should be remained unresolved when Lincoln was assassinated at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, dying the next morning.

Vice President Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Democrat and the only sitting Southern senator who had refused to join the Confederacy, succeeded Lincoln. Johnson had built his career attacking the planter aristocracy on behalf of poor white Southerners, and Radical Republicans initially hoped he would deal harshly with former Confederate leaders. He did not. Johnson's own Reconstruction plan, launched in the summer of 1865 while Congress was out of session, offered amnesty to most Confederates who took a loyalty oath, required states to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment, and required them to formally repudiate secession and Confederate war debts, but demanded little else. Johnson personally granted special pardons to thousands of wealthy planters and former officials who needed individual approval, restoring their property and political rights, and Southern voters soon elected former Confederate officials, including Alexander Stephens, the former vice president of the Confederacy, to Congress.

The results alarmed Republicans in Washington. State governments reorganized under Johnson's plan quickly passed the restrictive Black Codes, and the men elected to represent the South in Congress looked, in many cases, exactly like the prewar ruling class. When Congress reconvened in December 1865, Republican majorities refused to seat the newly elected Southern representatives and senators, rejecting Johnson's Reconstruction outright. That refusal marked the end of presidential control over Reconstruction and the beginning of a congressional takeover that would prove far more transformative, and far more contested, than anything Lincoln or Johnson had attempted.
